intelligence.human_view: A wall of text is a refusal to read. The reader unfold is the opposite shape: the full text, verbatim, but handed over one short paragraph at a time, each with a next button — the same unfolding mechanic as the deck, the same as the front page. The citizen never faces the whole thing at once, so they never feel overwhelmed; they click, click, click, and they are through it before they realize they have read it all. That is the point Shawn named: the tactic works because it never asks for the decision to read — it only asks for the next click. It becomes a common thing we do all the way through: anywhere a citizen would otherwise meet a wall — the agreement, the full contract behind the ⓘ, any long text — it unfolds instead. The text stays whole and verbatim; only the presentation changes. And the reader is beautiful: the words restated in the Naya Design way where they are ours to restate, plain to the average person, never bunched together.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine a really long story — but instead of one giant page that looks scary, you get one little bit at a time, and a magic button that says "next!" You tap, tap, tap — and before you know it, you've read the WHOLE story, and it was easy and fun!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — nobody wants to face a great big wall of words all at once, it puts you right off. So you give them a little bit at a time, one nice paragraph, and a button that says next. They tap, tap, tap, and before they know it they've read the whole thing, easy as anything. That's the kind way to show a long piece of writing.
intelligence.naya_view: Never a wall. One paragraph at a time, a next button each time — they click through it before they notice they have read it all. The text stays whole; only the presentation unfolds.
